name: Uma Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. Could you start by telling me a little about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Uma, 27. I'm a nurse on the postnatal ward at St Margaret's Hospital, so mums and babies in the first few days after birth. I did a two-year diploma and qualified just over a year ago. I live with my fiancé Pablo, who has his own carpentry workshop, and we're getting married next summer at our church. We've been careful with money; we've got about nine months of both our wages saved.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you? What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twelve-hour shifts. It's checking mums after caesareans, helping with feeding, weighing babies, spotting jaundice, and a lot of reassurance at three in the morning. Nothing beats a mum who's been crying all night finally getting her baby to feed. What wears me out is that I still miss things the midwives catch, and the discharge paperwork for each mum takes forever. I use AI on my phone every day, mostly to translate for mums who don't speak our language well and to check things I'm unsure of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a pity, because the little tools are genuinely helpful. I'd tell people at work about the translation app, because it's made a real difference for mums who don't speak our language. Online I'd say, don't throw out what works just because the hype was too big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. My job was always going to need hands and a calm voice, and I'd keep using AI for the small stuff. Maybe I'd be a little disappointed for Pablo, because he was hoping AI would help with his quotes and invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my shifts and do my breastfeeding support course in the spring. We'd go ahead with the wedding next summer and keep saving for a house. I'd help Pablo set up the small AI tools that do exist for his invoices anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, but happy with my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the translation app made a real difference. Can you give me an example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A young mum from abroad thought her baby's yellow skin meant something terrible. I used the app to explain jaundice and the light treatment, and she grabbed my hand. Before the translation app, we'd have waited an hour for an interpreter while a terrified mother sat crying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything on your mind about money or work in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Pablo's workshop is busy, there are three maternity units in the city, and we've got savings. The wedding costs make me wince, but that's a happy worry.

I'd tell colleagues about the **translation app** for mums who don't share our language.
think: My job always needed **hands** and a **calm voice**.
I'd feel a little **disappointed for Pablo**, who hoped AI would help his quotes.
do: Do my **breastfeeding support course** in the spring.
Go ahead with the **wedding** and keep saving for a house.
Set up small **invoice tools** for Pablo's workshop.
feel: **Calm**, a bit flat, but **happy** with my life.
S0.quote: Before the translation app, we'd have waited an hour for an interpreter while a terrified mother sat crying.
fieldNote: She already uses AI **daily** for translation and checks.
Her household has **two incomes**, one from a busy carpentry workshop.
The **wedding costs** are her only money worry.

steps.text: Take the breastfeeding support course on the postnatal ward in spring
Set up AI invoicing tools for her fiancé's carpentry workshop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for anyone willing to learn, and I'd say it to anyone who'd listen. At work I'd volunteer to show people how to use the new discharge tools. At church I'd tell the young people to get good with these tools early, like learning to drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's great for us. The AI can do my discharge paperwork, and I get more time with the mums. For Pablo, it means quotes, ordering timber and his accounts done in minutes, so he spends more time at the bench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up to be a digital champion on the postnatal ward and help write the guide for the new discharge system. I'd help Pablo bring in an AI tool for quotes and ordering in the first few months. And I'd think about running private antenatal classes on weekends, using AI to make the handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly excited. Like a door opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Private antenatal classes on top of twelve-hour shifts. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two Saturdays a month, in the church hall, for couples expecting their first. My mum ran a little cake business on top of her job for twenty years, so I grew up seeing that. It would be extra money for the house, and I love teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would struggle with these changes on your ward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the older midwives, who already roll their eyes at my phone. And the ward clerk, because discharge letters are half her job. I'd try to help them, but people have to want to learn.

I'd tell church youth to learn these tools **early, like driving**.

steps.text: Volunteer as digital champion and help write the discharge system guide

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge shake-up and families will need to pull together. I'd tell people to learn the tools fast and to look after each other, because I don't think governments will be quick enough. At church I'd want us to set up some kind of help for families who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it's mostly fine until 2031, because the paperwork goes but the hands-on care stays. Then robots arrive that can do some of the bed care, and Pablo's carpentry is hands-on work too. Robots that can cut and fit a kitchen would hit his workshop in the same year as my ward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first two years I'd help Pablo get ahead: buy one of the new robot cutting machines early, so his workshop becomes the one that uses robots, not the one beaten by them. I'd move toward the high-risk side of maternity, the sick mums and babies, where people want a real nurse. We'd keep the wedding but make it smaller and save the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited about some of it, but there's a knot in my stomach when I think about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a robot early is a big spend. How would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part from the wedding savings, part from a small business loan, and Pablo's dad might help. It's a risk, but I'd rather we owned the robot cutting machine than competed against it. If it went wrong, we'd still have my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a smaller wedding. How would your family take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would be upset for about a week, because she's been planning the menu since I was twelve. Then she'd say a marriage matters more than a party. We'd still have it at our church, just fewer cousins.

I'd want our **church** to set up help for families who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good amount of time if people are sensible. I'd tell my friends to start now, not in year four. At work I'd be running the sessions on the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd do well. Five years is enough for Pablo to bring robots into the workshop on his own terms and for me to get properly skilled in high-risk maternity. By 2034 we could have a house, a small business that uses robots, and maybe our first baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a high-risk maternity course in the next two years and keep the weekend antenatal classes going. I'd help Pablo plan a robot machine for the workshop around 2030, once prices drop. We'd have the full wedding next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy and hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a baby. Would the timing change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a year or two later than we'd hoped, so it's not in the middle of the workshop changes. But not much. Family comes first, and I want my children to see us building something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mums, honestly. Some of the young single mothers on my ward work in shops and call centres, which is the thinking work that goes in 2031. I'd want our church to help them, not just tell them to pray.

I'd tell friends to **start now**, not in year four.
think: Pablo can bring robots in **on his own terms**.
By 2034 we could have a **house, business and baby**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. I'd tell people at church to plan their children's education around it. Online I'd share good examples of people who've adapted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is the easy one for us. Pablo has a decade to grow the workshop and bring in machines slowly, and I'd be an experienced maternity nurse by 2039. Our kids would be little, and I'd want them learning both the tools and a craft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my courses one by one and maybe a degree top-up in midwifery, because midwives will always be needed at a birth. We'd buy a house in the next two years and start a family around thirty. I'd keep the antenatal classes as a small side business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and grateful. Like having the map before the journey.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why midwifery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've watched the midwives on our unit, and they carry women through the hardest day of their lives. A robot can hold a baby, maybe, but a frightened woman in labour wants a person she trusts. With ten years, I'd have time to train properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach your children, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To use the machines and to make things with their hands. Pablo would have them sanding wood by the time they're five. And to go to church, because that's where you find people when things change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both of us get hit in 2031, my ward and Pablo's workshop, before we've had kids or bought a house. What would help is cheap loans for small firms to buy the new machines, so people like Pablo can own them instead of being beaten by them. And hospitals training nurses for the skilled jobs that stay, like high-risk maternity and midwifery.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about small businesses. Everyone talks about big companies and robots, but a carpenter like my future husband, with one workshop, could use robots and AI too, if someone helped him get started. I'd want that help to exist.

headlineQuote: A carpenter like my future husband, with one workshop, could use robots and AI too, if someone helped him get started.
portrait: Uma, 27, is a **junior postnatal nurse** who uses AI daily, often to translate for mothers.
She's engaged to Pablo, a **carpenter** with his own workshop, and they have nine months saved.
Traditional and enterprising, she trusts **church, family** and small business over government.
Her instinct is to **own the robots**, helping Pablo automate before he's undercut.
With time she aims for **midwifery**; with two years she shrinks the wedding to fund the bet.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her ward and Pablo's workshop are both hit by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for small firms to buy the new machines.
Hospital training for **skilled roles** that stay, like high-risk maternity and midwifery.
